notes: Only open to sociology doctoral students.

description: Bi-weekly colloquium for graduate students that examines international migration and the incorporation of migrants into host societies. Students participate in meetings and present original work in progress.
notes: First class will be held

description: This seminar provides doctoral students in the Department of Sociology an opportunity to workshop drafts of their qualifying paper (QP). Submission of a satisfactory QP is required in order to progress to the dissertation project. The department expects the QP to be an original piece of research that is of publishable quality. Participants will receive different types of feedback on their projects throughout the semester: first, from the entire class when introducing the project; second, from the instructor in one on one meetings; and third, from two dedicated peer-reviewers who will comment on a full draft of the QP.
notes: Required of, and ordinarily limited to, third-year graduate students while writing the qualifying paper. Not repeatable for credit.

description: Professors Joscha Legewie and Robert Sampson are organizing the “Urban Data Lab” (UDL) to support research by students and postdocs examining the urban condition in the 21st century. The emphasis is on the active discussion of theoretical and empirical research that is in progress, in addition to occasional discussion sessions on selected readings to be determined by the group.
notes: Meets sporadically.

description: The Politics and Social Change Workshop facilitates the creation of an enduring, collaborative, and intellectually generative research community to investigate how politics shape social patterns in societies around the world. We define ‘politics’ broadly to include everything from politics within the household, to national domestic politics, to state politics within a transnational system. We meet every other week across the entire academic year. The goals of the workshop are to improve participants’ individual-level research projects, facilitate participants’ collaborative projects, and develop participants’ professional insights and policy-oriented expertise. To achieve these goals, we alternate between four types of activities: 1) hosting outside speakers, 2) providing feedback on graduate student or post-doctoral works, 3) professionalization sessions, and 4) collaborative discussions on cutting-edge research. The workshop is open to graduate students, post-doctoral fellows, and visiting scholars across Harvard. Students enrolling for graduate credit must attend every session and present their research at one session. Undergraduates are not eligible to enroll in this workshop for credit, but may attend with instructor permission. The course meeting schedule is below. To sign up for the workshop email list (or to remove your name from the list) please do so here or email psc-owner@lists.fas.harvard.edu.

The Workshop in History, Culture, and Society is a forum for the exploration of new developments in historical social science, especially in the fields of Anthropology, Economics, History, Political Science, Psychology, and Sociology. The workshop's primary methodological goal is to initiate a discussion of what constitutes acceptable historical evidence in each of the social sciences. Its main substantive goal is to understand how the past influences the present.

course_title: Contemporary Studies of Race & Ethnicity Workshop
description: The Contemporary Studies of Race & Ethnicity (CSRE) workshop's purpose is to provide a forum to disseminate knowledge and facilitate dialogue among graduate students, faculty, and visiting scholars working on or interested in research about contemporary studies related to race & ethnicity. Though the Sociology department hosts the workshop, we seek to bring scholars together across disciplines to explore topics such as ethno-racial hierarchies, racial attitudes, and intergroup relations, as well as the role of race in institutions, politics, and everyday life. The workshop will foster both a learning and collaborative space in which participants can circulate and garner feedback on works in progress, including dissertation chapters, proposals, journal article submissions, conference papers, and practice job talks.

current_sections.instructors: Daniel Schneider, Mary Waters, Xiang Zhou

description: The Social Demography Workshop is a venue for graduate students and faculty to present research on a wide variety of topics such as family, gender, inequality, im/migration, fertility, mortality, and the institutional arrangements that shape and respond to population processes.

course_title: Workshop on Work, Organizations, and Markets
description: Bi-weekly venue for graduate students engaged in macro- and meso-level organizational research. WOM is particularly valuable for students whose interests lie at the organizational environment, organizational, and work group/team levels. Students present original work in progress and provide commentary on presentations made by others.

The Contemporary Ethnography and Inequality Workshop advances cutting-edge, socially significant, and novel ethnographic work addressing social, economic, and political inequality. The workshop circulates, appraises, and critically evaluates research presented by leading scholars as well as works-in-progress by graduate students rigorously pursuing ethnographic inquiry and methods. The workshop is open to students and faculty from across the University as well as faculty and students from nearby Boston and Cambridge universities. While regular attendance is the norm, visitors are welcome.

The graduate workshop on Climate Sociology offers a venue for discussing new research that takes a sociological perspective toward climate change. Such perspectives include Environmental Sociology as well as areas of the field that have tended to develop independently of the problems of climate change, such as Social Organization, Social Stratification, Culture, Gender, Immigration, Political Sociology, and Race and Ethnicity. We encourage such disciplinary breadth of engagement in the problems of climate change because of the urgency of the climate crisis, and because we believe all sociologists can contribute to human knowledge about the causes and effects of climate change. For instance, although the topic of energy transition has been dominated by the physical sciences and economics, sociological insight into the forms of organizational ownership and control, the relationship between the rules of the game and the distribution of winners and losers, and the social meanings that attach to physical structures like oil wells and wind turbines all lead to more effective action on climate change. We welcome qualitative, quantitative, mixed-method, and applied research.

This workshop is a venue to discuss and receive feedback on on-going experimental research projects. The work presented and discussed will range from projects in the early stages of design and conceptualization through fully drafted manuscripts.
Individual work in sociology under the supervision of teaching staff in the department. A graded supervised course of reading and research on a topic not covered by regular courses of instruction.
notes: Students negotiate topics on their own. A final paper must be filed in the Sociology undergraduate office.

description: Students gain research skills along with an understanding of the production of sociological knowledge through work on faculty research projects.  Work is arranged and directed by faculty members, who supervise and meet with students regularly (every 1-2 weeks).  The specifics of the intellectual goals for the student and the research tasks involved will vary.  The student and faculty member will consult on this in advance and will outline the following on the 92r Registration Form:  1) the specific skills to be learned, 2) how the course will engage students with the discipline, and 3) the specific work product.  What students produce will depend on the kind of research involved.  It is expected that students will work 8 to 10 hours per week on the course.  Students may engage with data collection, data analysis, literature reviews, or other aspects of a faculty project.
notes: Members of the department.

description: This course introduces students to the complicated, conflictual, and often contradictory theoretical origins of sociology as a discipline.  We begin by reading the standard sociological “canon”—Marx, Weber, and Durkheim—and interrogating why their ideas were canonized over others.  We then read scholars who have been historically “written out” of the social sciences to evaluate their important, yet historically underappreciated, contributions.  By the end of the course, students should (1) master key concepts in classical sociological thought, (2) understand what it means to theorize, and what makes for good theory, and (3) learn to critically interrogate the relationship between power, standpoint, and the production of knowledge.
notes: Required of concentrators, ordinarily sophomores, and secondary concentrators.

course_title: Junior Tutorial: Deviance and Social Control
description: This course examines how institutions construct, enforce, and justify social control, shaping notions of deviance and conformity across historical and social contexts. From legal authorities to medical experts, we will explore how knowledge and power intersect to define who or what is considered “deviant” and how those labeled as such resist and reshape these boundaries. Topics include criminalization, surveillance, and the role of moral panics in reinforcing or challenging dominant narratives of social order. Students will choose a research question related to these issues and conduct their own empirical project using qualitative methods such as in-depth interviews, ethnographic observations, or textual/media analysis.

course_title: Junior Tutorial: Stigma and Social Recognition
description: This class examines how stigma — how having a “spoiled identity” (Goffman 1963) — shapes the way people act, interact, and make sense of the world. We will ask questions like: how do individuals or groups become stigmatized? How do people experience, cope with, or resist this stigma? How is stigma tied to discrimination, or the unequal access to resources and opportunities? And how might we reduce or challenge stigma? How can we promote its opposite, social recognition?Together, we will unpack the concept of stigma by diving into case studies. We will discuss the stigmas associated with dirty work, polluted relationships, illness, disability, poverty, criminal records, and more. We will also analyze the ways stigma intersects with class, race, gender, and sexuality. Our approach will be both micro-sociological — looking at individuals and social interactions — as well as meso-sociological — studying organizations, institutions, cultural scripts, and power.During the semester, you will also conduct your own research on stigma and recognition. You will learn to use and apply qualitative methods, either ethnography, participant observation, in-depth interviews, textual analysis, or archival work. You will also receive individualized support as you prepare your final project. By the end of the course, you will have a clearer sense of the mechanisms by which stigma contributes to social inequalities.

course_title: Junior Tutorial: Community in Urban Context
description: The notion of ‘community’ has long been central to the sociological study of cities and life within them. This course will familiarize students with what sociologists have written about the contours of urban community: what defines it, how it forms and persists, the functions it serves, and when it backfires. Through a mix of foundational and contemporary texts, the course will consider a number of the substantive issues that have historically shaped—and threatened—urban community, from social control to gentrification and city planning. During the semester, students will receive training in the use of ethnographic methods to study urban life and will conduct original research to answer questions of their choice about urban community (or an urban community).

course_title: Latin American Gothic: Literature and Film
description: The Gothic has become an inescapable and proliferating presence in contemporary culture. The global expansion of the term, its rather astonishing plasticity, has led experts to distinguish between categories such as Urban Gothic, Rural Gothic, Eco Gothic, War Gothic, Southern Gothic, and Tropical Gothic, among many others. Despite the world-wide nature of the phenomenon, however, the Latin American Gothic tradition still awaits further consideration. When did it make its first appearance and why? What are its chronological or developmental stages? Is it a product of foreign influence, an outgrowth of autochthonous conditions, or a combination of both? How is it related to magical realism, the folkloric legend, and the fantasy tale? How does it unfold in the hacienda or the convent, the jungle or the pampas, the plantation or the mines? How does it address the colonial, state, ecological, cultural, and racial violences that continue to afflict the region? The purpose of the course is to answer these and other pertinent questions through the examination of diverse primary sources (mostly literary works and films) and the theoretical writings of Gabriel Eljaiek-Rodríguez, Roger Luckhurst, and Nick Groom.

This intensive beginning class is for students with no previous formal training in Spanish, but with competence in at least one language other than English. In this class, students explore a host of social, cultural, and environmental issues that have historically impacted the lives and livelihoods of local, national, and foreign Spanish-speaking communities. Throughout the semester, students interact constantly with instructors, peers, and native Spanish speakers around the world as they explore culturally and linguistically rich content. Through discussions and critical analyses of authentic multimodal texts (e.g., written, audiovisual, visual) from many different sources (e.g., social media, newspapers), students develop a wide array of linguistic functions, such as the ability to make detailed descriptions or to narrate in different time frames. By the end of this class, students a) will have significantly advanced their linguistic competence, and b) will have deepened their understanding of the cultures and worldviews of Spanish-speaking communities in the United States, Latin America, and Spain.

description: Through novels that helped to consolidate nation-states in Latin America, explores modernity as personal and public lessons in laissez-faire. Sequels in film, telenovelas, performances show tenacity of genre. Links between creativity and citizenship. Theorists include Anderson, Foucault, Arendt, Lukacs, Flaubert.
notes: Conducted in Spanish.

course_title: Eloquent Instruments of God: Catholic Intellectuals in Latin America
description: In the course of five hundred years, the region now referred to as Latin America went from being the target of one of the most comprehensive evangelizing projects ever attempted, to becoming the Catholic Church’s strongest bastion. Far from static or monolithic, the richness, variety, and controversial character of such a long-lasting presence is reflected in the history of Latin American thought: among the many intellectuals influenced by Catholicism, one finds prophetic crusaders, poetic nuns, pious indigenists, radical liberals, reactionary antimoderns, authoritarian politicians, conservative feminists, ecclesiastical fascists, left-wing revolutionaries, and even a Pope. Catholicism has been, throughout the centuries, a never-ending source of inspiration for all sorts of intellectual traditions in the region.The objective of this course is to introduce students to Catholicism’s deep and lingering imprint in Latin America by means of a close-reading approach to some of its main intellectual figures, from the 15th century to the 21st. More than an institutional history of the Church, the course offers a survey of Latin American Catholic thought across the ages, focusing on its unceasing dynamism and intellectual heterogeneity. In terms of assigned readings, in-depth analysis of primary sources will be accompanied by contextualizing secondary literature.

Between 1923 and 1970, Jorge Luis Borges wrote some of the most original poems, short stories, essays and film scripts in Latin America and anywhere in the world, and he redefined the meaning and scope of literature. In this course, we will examine the signifying power of Borges’ short stories, essays and poems, and we will consider his work as a literary machine whose output radically transforms aesthetic formations and imaginaries beyond Argentina and Latin America. Rather than thinking about what his literature means, we will concentrate on what it produces as a fictional-poetic machine: cities and worlds, love and treason, popular and high culture, politics and death, institutions of knowledge and traditions, and new ways of reading and thinking about aesthetic and social relations.

course_title: Tears, Laughter, and Love: Affect and Popular Culture in Latin America
description: “What is love (baby don’t hurt me)?” pop culture keeps asking; in Latin America, one answer has long come in the form of tears, melodrama, and serialized romance. In the 1960s, the romance‑comic series Lágrimas, risas y amor promised its readers an education in how to suffer, laugh, and love. This course takes that archive of “tears, laughter, and love” as a point of departure to explore how Latin American popular culture has taught its publics to feel from the nineteenth century to the present. Primary materials will include sentimental poetry (Amado Nervo’s love poems), canonical and middlebrow fiction (María, Las batallas en el desierto, El beso de la mujer araña, En breve cárcel, Cuentos para leer sin rímel), women’s magazines from the nineteenth and twentieth centuries (La Mujer, Claudia, Para ti), and a range of audiovisual melodramas such as Enamorada, El crimen del Padre Amaro, El secreto de sus ojos, Una mujer fantástica, and telenovelas like Pasión de gavilanes, Rubí, and La reina del flow.Using “sentimental education” as a guiding thread, we will examine how affect participates in the making of gendered and classed hierarchies, ideals of love and family, and notions of respectability and taste in Latin America. Guiding questions include: How do material forms—cheap print, comics, magazines, film, and telenovelas—shape affective experience? What can affect theory and Latin American cultural criticism teach us about so‑called cursi or lowbrow genres? These case studies will be read alongside key texts in affect theory (e.g. Lauren Berlant, Sianne Ngai) and Latin American cultural theory (e.g. Carlos Monsiváis, Jesús Martín‑Barbero, Graciela Montaldo, Doris Sommer).
notes: Conducted in Spanish (readings in Spanish and English).  Designed as an introduction to the study of affect, materiality, and popular culture, the course is open to students from across the humanities and social sciences.

description: Data Science 1 is the first half of a one-year introduction to data science. The course focuses on the analysis of messy, real-life data to make predictions using statistical and machine learning methods. Material covered integrates the five key facets of an investigation using data: (1) data collection – data wrangling and cleaning to obtain a suitable dataset; (2) data management – accessing data quickly and reliably; (3) exploratory data analysis – generating hypotheses and building intuition; (4) prediction or statistical learning – developing and applying models such as linear and logistic regression, k-nearest neighbors, decision trees, and probabilistic approaches based on Bayes’ rule; and (5) communication – summarizing results through visualization, storytelling, and interpretable summaries.This is the first part of a two-course sequence. The curriculum builds throughout the academic year, and students are strongly encouraged to enroll in both the fall and spring courses within the same academic year.
notes: Only one of the following can be taken for credit: Stat 109a, Stat 121a, CS 109a, AC 209a.

description: Provides students a comprehensive understanding to the questions as of what is, how and why Bayesian. Introduction to classic Bayesian models, basic computational algorithms/methods for Bayesian inference, as well as their applications in various domain fields, and comparisons with classic Frequentist methods. As Bayesian inference finds its roots and merits particularly in application, this course puts great emphasis on enhancing students'  hands-on skills in statistical computation (mostly with R) and data analysis.

An in-depth introduction to statistical methods with linear models and related methods. Topics include group comparisons (t-based methods, non-parametric methods, bootstrapping, analysis of variance), linear regression models and their extensions (ordinary least squares, ridge, LASSO, weighted least squares, multi-level models), model checking and refinement, model selection, cross-validation. The probabilistic basis of all methods will be emphasized.

Statistical designs for efficient experimentation in the physical, life, social and management sciences and in engineering. A systematic approach to explore input-output relationships by deliberately manipulating input variables. Topics include completely randomized and randomized block designs, inferential adjustments for mulltiplicity of estimands, balanced incomplete block designs, factorial designs, confounding in blocks, fractional replications, and re-randomization. Each topic motivated by real-life examples.

Introduction to statistical approaches and methods for analyzing sports data, with a focus on estimating player and team strength.  Normal models for high-scoring games, Poisson models for low-scoring games, paired comparison models, regularized models and Bayesian approaches, multicompetitor models, dynamic models, rating systems, league and tournament simulation, regularized adjusted plus/minus, and Markov chains for evaluating game states. Emphasis will be on methodological underpinnings and on obtaining practical and interpretable results from data analysis.

description: This course delves into the intriguing realms of variations, information, and privacy, with a keen focus on both their qualitative conceptualizations, such as contextual integrity, and their quantitative specifications, exemplified by differential privacy. Our primary goal is to examine these concepts through a foundational statistical lens, and study statistics from the dual perspectives of creating and limiting information from data.At the heart of our exploration is the concept of variations, serving as a unifying theme that intricately links information (revelatory variations) with uncertainty (obfuscatory variations). This nuanced approach enables us to recognize that the principles governing how we restrict the flow of information mirror those involved in generating information (the traditional focus of statistics).A considerable portion of the course will focus on an in-depth study of differential privacy. First, we will dissect its mathematical framework through theory and examples, identify five key elements that define a general DP specification, and understand what it guarantees -- and what it does not. Second, we will delve into the intricacies of implementing DP via the case of the 2020 U.S. Census and the social and legal perspectives on privacy this raises. Third, we will learn about how to apply missing data methodologies to properly analyze differentially privatized data. Throughout the course, we will confront the challenge of meaningfully defining and quantifying individual privacy and information.By the conclusion of this course, students are expected to have developed a deeper appreciation for the complex interplay among variations, information, and privacy. They will be equipped with foundational analytical tools and statistical insights, empowering them to navigate the theoretical and practical challenges associated with revealing and concealing information in data for statistical inference and learning.

Random variables, measure theory, reasoning by representation. Families of distributions: Multivariate Normal, conjugate, marginals, mixtures. Conditional distributions and expectation. Convergence, laws of large numbers, central limit theorems, and martingales.

Foundations of frequentist and Bayesian inference, and decision theory. Likelihood, sufficiency, and ancillarity. Point estimation, unbiasedness, maximum likelihood, method of moments, minimum-variance. Parametric and non-parametric hypothesis testing, confidence intervals. Selective inference: multiple testing, familywise error rate, false discovery rate. Bayesian inference, conjugate priors, credible intervals. Admissibility, Stein's phenomenon, empirical Bayes. Time permitting: post-selection inference and the bootstrap.
notes: Formerly Stat 211a.

Bayesian theory, methods, and applications. Bayesian regression models, exponential family models, mixture models, and hierarchical models. Decision analysis and frequentist properties. Model checking and model comparison.

description: High dimensional data analysis is a recent interdisciplinary research area of Statistics, Genetics and Genomics, Engineering, and several other scientific areas. It addresses an array of challenging problems that of contemporary interest, and research in this area has been very active in the past decade.This course aims to provide a systematic introduction to various topics in high dimensional data analysis, focusing on large-scale sparse learning, and network and text data analysis. Large-scale sparse learning: Sparsity is a universal phenomenon in modern high dimensional data. Sparse structures are observed in many application settings and have many different forms, such as parameter sparsity, graph sparsity, eigenvalue sparsity, and so on. Exploring sparsity has become a common strategy in data analysis and has largely reshaped classical multivariate statistics problems. This course will investigate classical problems such as multiple testing, linear regression, classification and clustering, under the modern sparse settings. For each problem, the course discusses recent statistical methods for taking advantage of sparsity, and introduces thetheoretical framework for analyzing these methods.Network and text data analysis: Social networks and text documents are unconventional data types. This course introduces statistical models and methods for analyzing such type of data. Topics for network data analysis include community detection, mixed membership estimation, link prediction, and dynamic network modeling. Topics for text data analysis include topic modeling, word embedding, information retrieval, and sentiment analysis.

The theory and application of linear and generalized linear models, including linear models for normal responses, least-squares theory and inference, models for binary and multinomial data, log-linear models for count data, overdispersion and quasi-likelihood methods, model selection, and computational issues. Emphasizes the theory and development of methodology.

Substantive questions in empirical scientific and policy research are often causal. Does voter outreach increase turnout? Are job training programs effective? Can a universal health insurance program improve people's health? This class will introduce students to both statistical theory and applications of causal inference. As theoretical frameworks, we will discuss potential outcomes, causal graphs, randomization and model-based inference, sensitivity analysis, and partial identification. We will also cover various methodological tools including randomized experiments, regression discontinuity designs, matching, regression, instrumental variables, difference-in-differences, and dynamic causal models. The course will draw upon examples from political science, economics, education, public health, and other disciplines.

description: Recent advances in digital technology and artificial intelligence (AI) have fueled a revolution that is transforming science and society.  Massive data have been rapidly generated in many disciplines, such as genomics, health, physical and social sciences.  Scalable statistical machine learning (ML) and AI methods play a pivotal role in analyzing these data to ensure that scientific discoveries are reliable and trustworthy. This course focuses on cutting-edge statistical ML and AI methods. Discussions will be led by faculty members from the Departments of Statistics and Biostatistics, with active participation from students, postdoctoral fellows, and faculty. Students and postdoctoral fellows will collaborate with faculty on presentations that explore theoretical, methodological, and computational and application aspects of these areas.   The course will emphasize active discussions. Topics will include current research activities, challenges, and open problems. Example areas include ML methods, such as manifold learning, deep learning, representation learning, transfer learning, distributed and federated learning, contrastive learning, as well as generative AI methods such as large language models (LLMs), transformers, and diffusion models, and synthetic data. The integration of statistical and AI methods will also be highlighted. Applications of these methods across diverse scientific domains will be discussed.

With a multiplicity of references, PROJECT may refer to fundamental modes of architectural representation, the mapping of the human subject in the larger objective context, or a conceptual foray into territory yet unknown.A series of focused and intense design exercises requires students to investigate fundamental disciplinary issues of architectural thought, practice, and representation. As the introductory studio in the professional degree program, the curriculum addresses the varied educational backgrounds of incoming MArch I candidates. Students are encouraged to leverage their varied expertise in the sciences, humanities, and other disciplines to find provocative and unexpected motivations of architectural form and spatial thinking. Similarly, students are encouraged to draw parallels between studio and concurrent coursework in representation, history and theory, and the environmental sciences. The studio is a space for iterative exploration, and experimentation across various mediums such as drawing and modeling (both digitally and physically) will be required.Prerequisites: Enrollment in MArch I program.

course_title: Landscape Architecture I: First Semester Core Studio

current_sections.instructors: Zaneta Hong, Katherine Jenkins, Sonia Ralston

description: STU 1111 is the first in a sequence of four core studios that together establish the framework of the Master in Landscape Architecture program at the Harvard Graduate School of Design. Studio-based learning engages students in the practice of design as a synthetic and iterative process, integrating theory, technical knowledge, and aesthetic sensibility in the creation of landscapes. In this studio, students will apply the skills and knowledge developed through first-year coursework—including Histories of Landscape Architecture; Landscape Representation; and Ecologies, Techniques, Technologies—to the conceptualization and design of public spaces. Successful completion of this studio provides a critical basis for advanced study and professional practice throughout the remainder of the degree program.The central focus of the first-semester studio is landscapes of the public realm. What constitutes “the public”, and who has the authority to define it? What distinguishes a public landscape from a private one? How do we identify public space, and what forms of representation, governance, and funding sustain it?These questions will frame our work throughout the semester and will be explored through three interconnected themes that build progressively upon one another: landscapes as living matter; landscapes for equity and free assembly; and landscapes of recreation and public health.As a discipline concerned with the transformation and production of space, landscape architecture is fundamentally a materialist practice. Its outcomes are composed of physical matter, and design entails the deliberate transformation of living systems. This work requires a deep understanding of materials – their life cycles, modes of reproduction and decay, relationships with climate and weather, and ecological and cultural origins. As you develop fluency in working with materials, we will emphasize how the spatial configurations produced through landscape architecture generate consequences that extend beyond the physical realm. Landscapes shape and mediate relationships among organisms, people, and institutions, enabling certain forms of interaction while constraining others.In urban contexts, people are both the primary subjects and beneficiaries of these relationships. Public space occupies a particularly significant role as a domain for the expression and protection of democratic life. It is within public spaces that consequential forms of individual expression, collective action, and cultural exchange occur. Public landscapes therefore function not only as physical settings, but also as political and social infrastructures that support civic life.Following a brief introductory exercise focused on the fundamentals of materiality, the studio will investigate two types of public spaces common to many cities worldwide: the civic plaza and the waterfront park. Our sites of study will be Boston’s City Hall Plaza and Christian A. Herter Park along the Charles River in Allston. Through these projects, we will examine both the physical and political dimensions of landscape transformation. We will consider these sites as enablers of civic and human rights, as representations of shared conditions of existence, and as expressions of values, knowledge, and power. We will also attend to how every intervention in public space inevitably affirms, reshapes, or suppresses aspects of these shared conditions.

description: The studio will explore how we might reimagine cemetery landscapes of the future in response to the challenges of the climate crisis, and the clear and present issues of social inequality. These issues are extensively shifting the ways we live, and, at the very least, are the uninvited corollary through which we might imagine new expressions of the cemetery.As sites of remembrance, cemeteries may be considered as ‘places where memory crystalises and secretes itself as part of an ongoing construction of history’ (Pierre Nora 1989), whilst simultaneously acting as ‘settings in which memory is a real part of everyday experience’ (Michael Rothberg 2010). They are spaces that are socially produced and made productive in social practice (Lefebvre 1974), whilst also being highly logistical practical settings created in the absent presence of the body (Ken Warpole).Just as death is a necessary part of life, cemeteries are sites of contrast, yet it is perhaps through the very preservation of this tension of contradiction that they exist as some of the most enduring landscapes across cultures around the world.Often perceived as a space ‘apart’ from the city as a consequence of their physical traits and phenomenal characteristics, cemeteries none the less play significant roles within the life of the metropolis as biodiversity hotspots offering ecosystem services in the form of thermal regulation, stormwater management, and carbon absorption. They provide significant social functions such as spaces for people to seek sanctuary, reflection and play, and healthy spaces for individuals to contemplate in the context of a natural landscape.Cemeteries, capable and perhaps charged to carry multiple meanings, are paradoxical spaces described by Foucault (1967) as ‘heterotopias’, a no place that, nonetheless, is. The studio will be exploring what the urban and social significance of the cemetery of the future could be, and ask what are the forms and cultural expressions the urban cemetery might project? How might the articulation of the material and physical space reinterpret the temporal experience of the cemetery, and how might the increasingly rich cultural diversity of a progressive society be celebrated through ritual and mediated through disparate processes of burial and internment? How might the cemetery critique and address the extensive environmental and social issues that are before us by proposing alternative organisational patterns and expression, a place that celebrates diverse beliefs and rituals, and a space as an important contribution to the city’s natural systems?

course_title: First Semester Core Urban Planning Studio

current_sections.instructors: Hannah Teicher, Wendell Joseph, Timothy Love, Paola Aguirre Serrano, Carole Voulgaris

description: First Semester Core Urban Planning Studio introduces students to the fundamental knowledge and technical skills used by urban planners to investigate, analyze, create, and implement plans and projects.In this studio, Boston provides the location for developing skills and strategies to address and understand the local in its wider context. In planning the local area is of great importance and planners need to engage the particularities of districts, neighborhoods, towns, cities, and regions.Planners also understand and engage the wider context of places—in terms of physical scale, historical development, built character, social groupings, political structures, environmental attributes, economic activities, and future possibilities.The course focuses on key challenges of contemporary urban planning. The question of how planning can help make places more just and equitable is an enduring and foundational concern in planning. Towns and cities can help people gain access to nearby resources such as jobs, services, and cultural opportunities. For decades if not centuries, technological developments have expanded questions of access beyond the physical domain, a condition which seems to continually accelerate. The cross-cutting issues of equity and access will inform many aspects of the work throughout the semester.Major projects will engage with the challenges of affordability and climate change. Planners have had a longstanding concern with the effects of wealth and income inequality. While some elements of planning have accentuated growth dynamics that exacerbate inequality, other elements have played an active role in mitigating those effects, facilitating affordability and channeling the benefits of planning toward community well-being. Similarly, environmental planning has been a longstanding concern in the field. With accelerating climate disruptions, this concern has been evolving from a niche to the mainstream, where mitigating greenhouse gas emissions and adapting to impacts of climate change infuse many other domains of planning from housing, to transportation, to economic development.There are no easy answers; the critical and creative skills of the urban planner are being called upon now more than ever to advance the notion of a just and sustainable society.Planners address messy situations where the problems are disputed and the solutions contested. They identify issues, gather and analyze information, listen to opinions, draw on precedents, raise ethical concerns, and consider the future. They figure out the important questions to answer, engage stakeholders, propose strategies, communicate ideas, and create and revise proposals. In this studio students gain experience engaging with complex and unclear situations in ways that can lead toward plausible and ethical approaches to addressing them.The studio teaching approach is one of creating a setting for producing learning rather than delivering instruction about exactly what you should do. The process is collaborative and iterative. This can be a bit uncomfortable at first, but it is a low-risk environment. The assignments take you through a sequence of exercises that include reflection, analysis, proposal-making, and implementation while also addressing challenges (equity, access, affordability and climate). These occur at different scales and require both individual and group work.Students also experiment with how to effectively communicate with others using different visual, oral, and written techniques and media in pinups, slides, posters, and presentations.

description: The second semester core planning studio expands the topics and methodologies studied in the first semester core studio, GSD 1121, aiming to prepare students for the mix of analytical and creative problem-solving needed to be an effective planner. In this studio, students work on a real project in a real place (with a real client) that allows them to interact with the public; define a vision; collect, analyze, and represent data that supports that vision; develop a proposal that reflects public input; and present work in a sophisticated way that is relevant, legible, and useful to those who are not planners. By the end of the studio students will be familiar with a number of dimensions of community engagement, data analysis, plan making, and implementation.

description: Integration is the agenda for the third-semester architecture design studio. Architecture is fundamentally a part-to-whole problem, involving the complex integration of building components, systems, and processes into a synthetic whole. Structural systems, envelope design, and environmental and thermodynamic processes will be systematically addressed in the development of a single project during the course of the whole semester.The building type consists of a multiprogram urban building, requiring careful consideration of access and exchanges (circulatory, visual, and energy), between programs. During that time students will work in consultation with engineers and scientists. Design exercises will be addressed through team and individual study.Prerequisites: STU 1101 and STU 1102, or advanced standing in the MArch I program.

description: The fourth and final semester of the core sequence, this architecture studio tackles the complexity of the urban condition through the design of housing. From individual to collective, from spatial to infrastructural,  from units to systems, housing not only confronts the multiple scales of design but also exposes the values and ideals of its society. The semester will be an opportunity to imagine the possible futures of the city, recognizing the role of architecture at the intersection of the many interdependent as well as contradictory forces at play, and the negotiations that must necessarily take place. The semester will be organized in two overlapping phases. The first weeks will be an intense research and analysis phase through which the students will develop not only an understanding of historical precedents but also begin to formulate their narrative on urban living – a hypothesis that they will use to launch their design for the rest of the semester. While this hypothesis will be constantly revisited and revised, it will serve as a first speculative act.The second phase of the semester will be devoted to the elaboration of an urban project with a focus on housing and will have as its objective the understanding of design as a series of relativities: between building and the city, between collective and individual, between civic and domestic. The architectural project is fundamentally optimistic. It goes beyond problem solving to imagining a better future. In no other typology is this more true than with collective housing which defines the core of how we live and function together as a society.Pedagogically, working in groups and pairs will be a component of the semester, demanding dialogue, understanding, and negotiation of different points of view.

course_title: Landscape Architecture III: Third Semester Core Studio

current_sections.instructors: Chris Reed, Karen Lee Bar-Sinai, Francesca Benedetto, Rosalea Monacella, Amy Whitesides, Slide Kelly

description: Wild Entanglements / Living With, Living AlongsideMetropolitan Boston This studio focuses on designing for human | non-human relations at the metropolitan periphery, on both local sites and within regional networks. In doing so, it explores themes of connectivity, resilience, and entanglement through the lens of wildlife and landscape infrastructure projects. The projects that emerge from this work will re-establish wildlife habitat in the context of dynamic human settlements and spaces, subject to water flows and flooding, and will offer accommodation for people (access, movement, gathering) in relationship to wild creatures and forces.Our work will be grounded in the intertwined challenges of the global polycrisis, i.e. climate change and biodiversity loss in the Anthropocene. We will engage conversations, projects and precedents that address our relationships to other species and the environments we share and on which our futures depend—and that operate across the scale of the metropolis. We will consider new and reciprocal relationships with the creatures that co-exist with us—exploring the implications of living with and living alongside those creatures and forces that exist in the world beyond our immediate human selves. We will explore the conceptualization and development of new hybrid assemblages, new infrastructural ecologies, new imaginaries that foster deeper relations, entanglements, and kinships between and among all of earth’s inhabitants. And we will do so on the remains of a peri-urban site, at the confluence of two altered rivers, in the context of existing, denuded, and former ecological and social networks in ways that re-establish space for water, wildlife, and people in relationship to—and in dialogue with—one another.Importantly, this is not an anti-human endeavor; rather, and perhaps most profoundly, it an attempt to re-establish connections, re-affirm the culture of nature, re-embrace the living world, and re-engage us as social and ecological creatures through the multiple lenses of all who dwell among us.We will draw on the writings and research of naturalists, ecologists, and theorists such as Jennifer Wolch, Donna Haraway, Robin Kimmerer, Timothy Morton, Erle Ellis, Nina-Marie Lister and others. We will study projects and projections for metropolitan landscape systems and infrastructure by innovative planners and designers, including Charles Eliot and Sylvester Baxter, James Corner, Anuradha Mathur and Dilip da Cunha, Matthew Gandy, the Dutch Government, and Yu Kongjian. And we will engage physical, temporal, and geo-spatial modeling tools that will allow us to explore multi-dimensional aspects of time, space, and scale.

current_sections.instructors: Lorena Bello Gomez, Karen Lee Bar-Sinai, Francesca Benedetto, Danielle Choi, Zaneta Hong, Max Piana

description: The Near Future CityThe fourth and final semester for the core Landscape Architecture sequence responds to our most pressing urban agenda in the years to come to transition into climatically just and resilient cities where no-one is left behind. As a Landscape Architect your role in this urban climatic transition is fundamental. Core IV provides you with the tools and skills to translate the important values and actions embedded in this process, into individual design proposals that are specific and concrete for the city of Boston.Core 4 joins efforts from the international, state, municipal, and civil society to accomplish this needed task. Among others: the Paris Agreement; State’s ResilientMass Plan; Mayor Michelle Wu’s Boston Green New Deal & Just Recovery synthesizing many of the Boston Climate Resilience initiatives toward climate adaptation and decarbonization; or EPA and the Mystic River Watershed Association to reduce pollution.The semester opens with an immersive pre-term symposium to learn first-hand from state, city officials, and NGOs on their multiple Boston plans, initiatives, and policies while experts share important precedents and critically assess the encounters. As an academic exercise, we will have the freedom to move beyond the “status quo” of present possibilities, to more desirable outcomes toward climatic resilience in the Near Future. While enhancing your imagination in the creative process of design, this might be precisely where our collaboration becomes more nurturing and catalyzing.After the opening, the semester is structured around three ACTIONS: 01. analyzing; 02. spatializing; 03. projecting. Each ACTION combines expert lectures, readings, skill building workshops, and exercises that built sequentially and iteratively upon each other during the semester. In closing, students assembled their work for a Near Future Charlestown Presentation to continue the engaging conversation that was started at the opening symposium.

description: Elements of Urban Design is the required first semester advanced core studio for the post-professional Urban Design Program. Regarding learning objectives, the studio introduces critical concepts, strategies and technical skills associated with thinking about Urban Design and allows speculation on a designer’s spectrum of roles in shaping urban environments. More generally the studio aims to develop necessary literacies for architects and landscape architects to engage in the bridging practice of Urban Design and to understand questions related to urban environments and to produce compelling formal responses. Here a fundamental difference between Urban Design and Architecture and Planning is its concern for the ‘thingness’ in a Heideggerian sense, of urban settlement, which transcends the single building complex and involves competing claims and other unreconciled constraints needing to be resolved through design. Typically, cities are often parts of larger networks of communities and ecologies with both overlapping and complementary roles. Urban growth and change now range over a wider landscape, offering both opportunities, constraints and outcomes located in peri-urban, peripheral, and central locations. Within the scope and content of the studio, consisting of two Urban Design problems, each subdivided into exercises, evaluative reviews and crits will be accomplished by a series of fourteen presentations across topics within the two problems. Structural racism and effects of the Anthropocene Era, along with concomitant institutional issues and biases will be engaged with each specific exercise but also more generally through adherence to social actions, environmental awareness, and a cosmopolitan outlook. More specifically, in the first problem and exercises dealing with East Boston, housing affordability and other forms of discrimination will be challenged and discussed, along with the matter of Climate Change and sea-level rise. Similarly, in peripheral developments like Westwood in the second problem, the matter of access as well as environmental suitability will be topics of consideration. Throughout a sequence of topical presentations will be provided in an asynchronous format on these and related topics, including brownfield site amelioration, sea-level rise, landscape ecology, storm-water management, urban justice, and various forms of spatial development. The other first-term required course for incoming Urban Designers, titled GSD 4496 Urban Desing Contexts and Operations, will also bear on many of these and related topics.

Bridging quantitative analysis, computational methodologies, and systemic design, students learn through continuous, iterative making.Operating at the frontier of the natural and the artificial, the curriculum pushes students beyond their existing disciplinary boundaries. The semester demands a high tolerance for ambiguity as students tackle novel AI systems forensics, synthesize massive global datasets, and engineer robust, field-deployed mechatronics to address complex global challenges.This studio is limited to first-year students enrolled in the Master in Design Engineering program, a collaborative degree associated with the Harvard GSD and SEAS.
course_requirements: GSD: MDE students

current_sections.instructors: Elizabeth Christoforetti, Leighton Beaman, Justin Cook, Mark Coughlin, Monique Fuchs, George Guida, Karen Reuther, Daniel Tish

description: The second-semester studio builds upon theoretical and technical concepts already introduced in the MDE program, emphasizing problem assessment, creative and critical thinking, observational and experimentation-based evaluation, and context-aware communication strategies essential for complex problem-solving activities. Within the scope of the 2D, 3D, and 4D MDE studio pedagogy, the fourth dimension, time, will feature strongly in project considerations. Students will be challenged to prioritize deeper reflection and holistic connections across the entire ecology of their design-engineering project (i.e. systems design, experiential design, futuring, and large-scale thermodynamics).This year, student teams will develop a semester-long project on “Water as a System of Care” through one of  three human-centric-scales: IN the body (i.e., medicine, nutrition, drinking, TOUCHING the body (i.e. fashion, beauty, recreation, thermal health), or AROUND the body ( i.e., infrastructure, transportation, construction). Student teams will develop product-based solutions leveraging an interdisciplinary approach that blends design thinking with insights from economics, sociology, technology, and public policy. Collaboration with experts across these fields, as well as with the communities that will be affected by these changes, will be vital in developing human-centric solutions that are truly desirable, feasible, and tangible.This Studio is limited to first-year students enrolled in the Master in Design Engineering Program, a collaborative degree program associated with Harvard GSD and SEAS.

The studio tackles the pressing need to rethink and repurpose the machine-like hospital building constructed in the decades following World War II. In America alone, thousands of these buildings were built following the passage of the 1947 Hill-Burton Act. These structures, once at the forefront of clinical architecture, have become outdated as medical practice and technology have progressed and hospital design has evolved to prioritize patient-centered care, new technical standards, and community integration. In an era where minimizing our carbon footprint is paramount, the adaptive reuse of existing buildings offers a sustainable alternative for certain aspects of hospital construction. This studio addresses a global challenge with a local solution, transforming an outdated hospital building into a rehabilitated place of care.Building on knowledge collected during a visit to see Herzog & de Meuron’s hospitals and other relevant work in Switzerland, students will develop a proposal for the adaptive reuse of one of Boston’s most prominent hospital buildings. The studio focuses on the Massachusetts Eye and Ear Tower at Massachusetts General Brigham Hospital in Boston. The Tower, now approaching the end of its useful lifespan, presents an opportunity for creative intervention. To repurpose it, students will be asked to incorporate a neuro-rehabilitation center and to propose an additional programmatic element that enhances the building’s functionality, connectivity to the overall hospital and community relevance.Hospitals should no longer be considered isolated campuses for the ill, but integral parts of our cities that serve the entire community. Rehabilitation for the mind and for the body are considered. Key themes are adaptive reuse, urban transformation, community placemaking, and the relationship between the human body and its surroundings.Following the analytical phase, students will develop a concept for the adaptive reuse of the selected building. This design process will operate at three distinct scales: the macro scale of the hospital and city, the intermediary scale of the existing building, and the micro scale of a single patient related space. Students will be encouraged to explore innovative design solutions that address the complex interplay between these scales, ensuring that the final proposal is both visionary and practical.By the end of the course, students will have developed a comprehensive proposal that not only revitalizes an outdated hospital building but also contributes to the broader discourse on sustainable urban development and healthcare architecture. This design studio offers a unique opportunity to explore the intersection of architecture, urbanism, and healthcare, equipping students with the skills and insights needed to address the challenges of one of our most crucial but underappreciated building typologies.This studio is supported by the AECOM Design Research Fund.

course_title: Shared City: Subverting Positive / Negative Space
description: The studio examines housing as a critical instrument in the production of urban form and collective life. Led by Johanna Hurme + Saša Radulovic of 5468796 Architecture, the course investigates the agency of architecture within broader social, political, economic, and cultural systems, with particular attention to the role of shared space in shaping collective forms of inhabitation.The studio begins with a critical examination of prevailing North American housing models and the assumptions that underpin contemporary residential development. Particular attention is directed toward the spaces between buildings and the role they play in structuring social relationships, environmental performance, and everyday urban life.Central to the studio is the proposition that the “in-between” spaces: courtyards, mews, yards, passages, and shared outdoor domains constitute an essential form of social and environmental infrastructure.Rather than functioning as residual space, these environments mediate relationships between public and private realms, support social interaction, contribute to ecological performance, and shape patterns of collective inhabitation. The studio places particular emphasis on northern contexts, where climatic conditions and seasonality present unique challenges and opportunities for the design of shared space.Students will study housing systems that integrate architecture, public policy, planning, and development practices to support socially cohesive urban environments. Topics include mixed-tenure housing, anti-segregation planning, affordable, cooperative and collective housing models, density and the relationship between housing form and the public realm. Housing is positioned not merely as a building type, but as a socio-spatial framework through which broader questions of equity, governance, sustainability, and urban citizenship can be explored.Students will engage the subject through lectures, readings, precedent and case-study analysis, site research, density studies, physical and analytical modelling, programmatic and conceptual design exercises, and iterative design development. A field study in Helsinki will provide direct exposure to significant housing projects, urban districts, architectural practices, and public agencies, offering a comparative perspective on Finnish/North American approaches to housing and collective urban space.Final outcomes will consist of physical models, analytical drawings, two- and three-dimensional representations, and film-based documentation. Evaluation will be based equally on conceptual clarity and intellectual rigor, depth of investigation, quality of process and design development, craft and precision of representation, and effectiveness of communication and presentation.This studio is supported by the Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies.

course_title: WIND AND WATER Infrastructures for the Wild Atlantic Way
description: For many rural populations, tourism offers an economic opportunity, but it can also stifle the development of a living place. Rural landscapes, historic towns, and cities, can become “living museums.” The changes that modern life brings can make the image of a place unpalatable.The focus of this studio is a rural landscape in western Ireland. Central to the ethos is the understanding of the place as an inhabited landscape, a landscape from which and within which people make a livelihood and a life. We propose to move past the landscape as “scenic” to investigate how design can contribute to making these rural areas vital again.The region, at one of Europe’s most westerly points, has a rugged and heavily indented coastline shaped by the Atlantic Ocean. Poor agricultural land, and a lack of connectedness and opportunity, have historically contributed to extensive depopulation and the west currently depends heavily on tourism for economic opportunity. The Wild Atlantic Way is a structured rebranding of existing roads that follow this exposed coastline along the length of Ireland’s west coast. As the name suggests, the Wild Atlantic Way is exposed to some of the highest wind speeds in Europe. Wind energy is widely regarded as Ireland’s surest path towards energy self-sufficiency. Currently 40% of Ireland’s electricity is generated from wind energy with a goal to achieve 80% from renewable sources by 2030.Bringing together the often opposing physical and economic forces of tourism and energy production, the studio will create a research station for wind and wave energy and a tourist hub. The studio will visit the west coast of Ireland and travel some of the Wild Atlantic Way.Patterns of rural development in the west are dispersed with new population loads posing challenges for infrastructure, most significantly and counter-intuitively, for water. We will investigate how to design with no or limited water/sanitation infrastructure and the implications for land use. This studio focuses on building in this landscape and this place. We will begin by reviewing strategies undertaken in other locations around the world. A short introduction project on water will begin the design process.Student work will be evaluated based on their demonstration of a comprehensive understanding of the various pressures of the project, as well as how their project reinvents the place. A comprehensive understanding and approach to the site is essential. This studio utilizes both landscape architecture and architecture skills.This studio is supported by the Koji Yanai Innovative Infrastructure Initiative Fund.

course_title: Afterlives: Transforming Saarinen’s Ellinikon Terminal, Museum of Design Athens
description: Obsolescence and reuse are the focus of the Afterlives studio. Architecture is often imagined as a process of formation, of construction — architecture’s debut. The other end of the process is often overlooked — its demise. What happens to architecture after its uses change, and its occupants move out, and the technology shifts, and no one cares for it anymore? What happens to architecture after it is rendered obsolete? The notion of obsolescence is integrally tied to notions of modernity and progress. Demolition is the corollary to construction, just as obsolescence is the flip side of modernity. Architectural historian Daniel Abramson argues that obsolescence is integral to understanding architecture under capitalism. Architecture is recast not only as a means of wealth creation as a real estate commodity, but also as a depreciating asset. Modernity also relies on the concept of obsolescence as an essential component of process.The Ellinikon Terminal in Athens, designed by Eero Saarinen, operated for 44 years before being rendered obsolete in 2001. Saarinen designed the Athens terminal building shortly after the TWA Terminal at JFK (1962) and Dulles Airport outside Washington DC (1962). The Ellinikon terminal was designed as a modern Pergamon Altar for the jet age. Drawing from classical models, Saarinen sketched a raised platform rising from the “landside” of the airport and gesturing to the runways as a viewing deck from which to wave to arriving planes and catch a glimpse of the future.The Ellinikon Airport is currently being redeveloped as a 1,500-acre mixed-use coastal park and neighborhood including residential, commercial, and sports facilities by LAMDA Development. The Afterlives studio scenario involves the speculative reuse of the Saarinen Terminal building as the future home of the new Museum of Design Athens (MODA).The founders of MODA see design as a transformational force within culture. Design shapes ways of thinking about the world, actively, as an activity of imagining alternative worlds. With this agenda in mind, the MODA will not be a passive museum for housing objects on pedestals, but rather a place to the exchange of ideas — prompted by the presence of design objects. A place for convening, for test driving concepts, making connections and for speculating on futures.Students will work on proposals to transform the Saarinen terminal into a new type of cultural institution. Students will develop concepts for exhibitions and curatorial positions vis a vis the existing building, developing a parallel between the container and its contents. The studio includes travel to Athens, as well as local trips to the MIT Museum, its storage facility, and meetings with curators, exhibition designers, and historic preservation experts.This studio is supported by Hellinikon S.M.S.A.

This studio asks students to investigate the relationship between the city, architecture, and public space, with the goal of producing a critical reflection and subsequently developing design proposals intended to demonstrate architecture’s capacity to shape, redefine, and activate public space. The assignment is a proposed design of a mixed-use complex in three urban nodes within the central archaeological area in Rome. The three selected areas present similar urban, architectural, morphological, and topographical challenges. Underlying the course is a reflection on the concept of palimpsest: students will reflect on the presence of the various traces that have accumulated over time and on the role of memory within such a significant place.Rome’s central archaeological area, the symbolic heart and physical center of the city, is the focus of renewed and intense interest from both public administration and the general public. This interest stems from the fact that this area, arranged during the Fascist regime as a grand stage set designed primarily to showcase the empire’s magnificence, no longer serves as the civic and symbolic center of the city, despite its geographical centrality. Overrun daily by hundreds of thousands of tourists, lacking adequate services for both residents and visitors, and poorly connected to the rest of the city, this area risks becoming a “black hole” within the city. Students will consider how they can contribute to returning this part of the city to its citizens by transforming the central archaeological area into a large and multifaceted system of public spaces.The result of the studio will be a complete development of a project in all its different aspects and scales, from urban settlement to architectural definition. The design process will be structured in four phases— analysis of the site, definition of the program, definition of project’s structure, and the final project—allowing for a detailed analysis of the various steps. Students will develop different working hypotheses on the proposed topic and through texts, drawings, sketches, models, and diagrams will demonstrate a critical understanding of the topic shown in the final deliverables.Student evaluation will consider the overall ability to address the themes and questions raised by the studio. Attention will be given to comprehension of the site, environment, and context; ability to interpret the given functional program based on their understanding of the topic; development of analytical and interpretative skills; connection of abstract ideas to real architectural proposals; and development of representational and communication skills.This studio is supported by the Kenzō Tange Visiting Chair in Architecture and Urban Design.

course_title: Before the Master Plan: Architecture as Cultural Hypothesis for Shinagawa Ura, Tokyo
description: Over the past two decades, a sameness has emerged in the physical form of urban development. Districts in Boston, London, Singapore, and elsewhere increasingly share the same planning logic, building types, public spaces, and aesthetic language. While these models have proven effective at attracting initial real estate investment, they have also produced a growing architectural self-similarity that weakens local identity, limits cultural imagination, and ultimately diminishes the long-term value of place.This studio begins from the proposition that architecture possesses greater agency than contemporary development models allow. Rather than understanding buildings as the products of master planning, students will treat architecture as a mode of inquiry capable of revealing alternative futures for the contemporary city. Working at the scale of buildings, their immediate public realm, and the human experience between them, students will formulate fundamentally architectural hypotheses: design propositions that ask how specific forms, types, and spatial relationships might generate new modes of public life, cultural identity, and urban value. Tokyo’s Shinagawa Ura serves as the laboratory through which these hypotheses are developed and tested, building upon the research established in the GSD spring 2026 research seminar Contingent Grounds: Site Analysis for the 21st Century.This premise challenges the prevailing logic of contemporary urban development. Modern innovation districts are typically conceived from the top down: economics produces the master plan, the master plan produces buildings, and buildings produce experience. This studio reverses that sequence. Beginning with architectural form and human experience, students will speculate on the cultural DNA from which an urban district—and ultimately new forms of cultural value—might emerge. Working from the bottom up rather than the top down, architecture becomes the medium through which the identity of a place is imagined before it is codified as a master plan.This methodological inversion reflects a broader proposition about the role of design itself. Contemporary development practice often assumes that value can be determined before design begins, with architecture serving primarily to realize economic and planning objectives. The studio advances an alternative position: architecture is not simply the product of urban development; it is the instrument through which new forms of urbanism are discovered. Design is understood not as the execution of a predetermined vision, but as a mode of research capable of revealing latent cultural, spatial, civic, and economic possibilities whose “value” cannot be fully anticipated through finance, planning, or market analysis alone.The studio is conceived as a collaboration with NSKRE, the master developers of the Shinagawa Ura district site, as they imagine and construct its future in real time. Embodying a spirit of radical pragmatism, the studio poses an opportunity for students to explore the potential of civic architecture with real-world implications, constraints, and live stakeholders. Travel to Tokyo will occur during the week of October 5th.This studio is supported by the NSKRE Studio Fund.

Between roughly 1950 and 1970, New York produced the most coherent body of commercial architecture in its history. Lever House and Seagram established the type, the 1961 Zoning Resolution codified the plaza that came with it, and within two decades several hundred towers were built on that logic, most of them competent, a few of them extraordinary, and only a handful of them landmarked. This studio takes that inventory as its subject. The buildings are structurally sound and superbly located, and increasingly unwanted, having been designed around a pattern of work that no longer exists. Demolishing them writes off the carbon already spent and leaving them alone writes off the site.The regulatory moment is favorable in a way it has not been. City of Yes for Housing Opportunity zoning amendment widened conversion eligibility to buildings completed before 1990 and, through the Universal Affordability Preference, exchanges additional residential floor area for permanent affordability. New York State's Affordable Housing from Commercial Conversions tax incentive rewards commercial to residential conversion where a quarter of the units are income restricted. The 2025 state energy code, the first in the country to require most new buildings to be all electric, sets a performance floor that no 1960s envelope can meet without substantial intervention.Students will work in pairs. During the field trip we will collectively shortlist four buildings, each taken up by two pairs working independently, so that every host yields two distinct propositions. Each pair determines the programmatic mix and defends it. The common frame is office converted principally to housing, with 25 percent affordable units, a 25 percent floor area increment earned in exchange, a community facility, and a reasonable measure of at-grade retail. Every residential unit should be tested for private outdoor space, whether balcony, terrace or loggia, and each project should propose a set of shared residential amenities. Structure, core and envelope are the given conditions, and they are open to being worked on. This is an experimental design studio, and formal exploration is encouraged across addition, subtraction, surfacing, and spatial invention, from volume excavated out of deep plans to the massing and expression of the overbuild itself.The work rests on shared research. We will build a collective base covering current code, zoning, incentives, energy requirements, construction cost, and sell-side economics, so that each pair designs against real numbers rather than assumptions. The field trip combines walking tours with survey and documentation.The premise is that carbon, cost, code, and architecture are one problem, that it rewards experimentation, and that these buildings, which carry real cultural value, are best served by a repositioning that answers how people live and work in the city now.

For decades, architecture has pursued performance through optimization: more efficient, more precise, more controlled. This model relies on complex systems operating under stable conditions. As climate uncertainty and resource scarcity transform the environments in which buildings operate, this paradigm reveals its limits. Buildings optimized for stability often prove the least capable of accommodating change.The studio proposes robustness as a new understanding of architectural performance. It asks how performance might be redefined—not as the maximization of efficiency, but as the capacity to absorb uncertainty. Robustness privileges redundancy over precision, repair over replacement, and adaptability over permanence.Corporate office buildings provide a critical ground on which to test this shift. Built at an unprecedented scale and increasingly challenged by declining occupancy, they are among the building types most exposed to premature obsolescence. They depend on intensive mechanical systems and continuous maintenance, making them vulnerable to climate change and rising operating costs.The studio investigates how new climatic artifacts within existing buildings can challenge conventional approaches to adaptive reuse. Rather than programmatic change, proposals emerge from the interaction between climate, context, and low-tech climate systems.Brussels, home to the European Commission, contains 12.5 million m² of office space for 1.2 million inhabitants—one of Europe’s highest office-space-per-capita ratios. The studio trip will combine an in-depth understanding of the case study with meetings and discussions involving the various actors engaged in the transformation of these buildings. Much of this stock now faces premature obsolescence, while its ongoing transformation has typically relied on energy- and resource-intensive renovations.Guided by an economy of means, the studio will instead explore selective, resource-conscious approaches. Drawing on Layers of Change, we will read the building anatomically, assessing each component by its lifespan and adaptive potential. Prioritizing in situ reuse, we will repurpose existing components into new climatic artefacts.Rather than transforming the whole building, the studio will identify where limited interventions can produce the greatest architectural and climatic impact. We will develop climatic prototypes as architectural interventions evaluated through digital modeling and CGI imagery.Ultimately, the question is architectural: how does shift in value—from optimized objects to robust artifacts—reframe our understanding of new ways of living?This studio is supported by the John Portman Visiting Chair in Architecture.

course_title: Housing as an Ecology of Care: From Blank Type to Dwelling
description: This studio explores housing as an ecology of care, a framework that understands architecture as a relational practice embedded in networks of interdependence among people, species, systems, and time. In this view, a multi-story residential building is a place to live as well as to heal, connect, and coexist—a dwelling for human and nonhuman life.We will apply this lens to the transformation of an existing department store, the GALERIA Berlin Hermannplatz, an example of a building type that has shaped city centers in Europe and North America for over a century but which now faces obsolescence in the e-commerce era. The department store is the archetypal blank type: its facade bears no relationship to its interior, its depth exceeds what any habitable program can tolerate, and its spaces are organized around the display and movement of goods rather than people. Working within these constraints, we will approach the conversion of this blank type through five overlapping domains of care:Historical care preserves and reinterprets the building’s embedded history while avoiding the carbon cost of demolition. Integrating extant features such as atriums, escalators, and elevator and stair cores allows past labor and use to inform future dwellings.Planetary care explores how the deep, column-free floor plate that makes housing difficult can be opened to support human and non-human life, becoming an interior garden, light well, inhabited courtyard, or green roof.Social care asks how the store's spatial generosity—its wide corridors, open floors, and open ground-level—can be reworked to form an architecture of collective life that is also deeply connected to nonhuman life.
